title: RF Spectrum Overview
body: The usable radio spectrum for a wideband receiver like a Malahit spans roughly 100 kHz to 2+ GHz depending on the model. Moving up in frequency: LF/MF holds AM broadcast; HF (3–30 MHz) is where shortwave and most amateur long-distance activity lives; VHF (30–300 MHz) covers FM broadcast, airband, 2m ham, marine, and NOAA Weather Radio; UHF (300 MHz–3 GHz) covers 70cm ham, GMRS/FRS, and much more. As a rule of thumb: lower frequencies travel farther via ionospheric ‘skywave’ bounce (especially at night) but need longer antennas and carry more atmospheric noise; higher frequencies are mostly line-of-sight, cleaner, and use much smaller antennas.

title: HF vs VHF vs UHF
body: HF (High Frequency, 3–30 MHz) can travel worldwide by bouncing off the ionosphere ('skywave'), especially at night - this is how shortwave broadcast and long-distance amateur contacts work, but it also brings more static and fading. VHF (Very High Frequency, 30–300 MHz) is mostly line-of-sight - range is limited by antenna height and terrain, not time of day - and is generally quieter; this is where FM broadcast, airband, 2m ham, marine VHF, and NOAA Weather Radio live. UHF (Ultra High Frequency, 300 MHz–3 GHz) is also line-of-sight, typically shorter range than VHF for the same power, but antennas are much smaller; this is where 70cm ham, GMRS, and FRS live.

title: HF Propagation Basics
body: HF signals can travel very long distances by refracting off the ionosphere back down to earth ('skywave'), but how well this works depends heavily on time of day, season, and the 11-year solar cycle. During the day, the lowest HF bands (160m/80m) are absorbed by the lower ionosphere and mostly limited to short range; at night that absorbing layer disappears and those same bands can suddenly carry much farther. Higher HF bands (20m/17m/15m/12m/10m) tend to work better in daytime and can go quiet at night. None of this is exact - solar activity, season, and geography all shift the picture, so the practical approach with a wideband receiver is simply to check several HF bands at different times of day and see what's actually open right now.

title: Antenna & Band Guidance
body: An antenna generally works best when its physical length relates simply to the wavelength of the frequency it's used on - lower frequencies need physically longer antennas for the same efficiency. The short telescoping whip that comes with most wideband receivers is a broad compromise that isn't well-matched to any single band, which is especially noticeable on HF (a longer wire antenna, even just tossed out a window, usually improves HF reception dramatically). VHF/UHF reception benefits less dramatically from a bigger antenna since local transmitters (repeaters, airband, marine, NOAA) are often strong enough to hear well on the stock antenna, though orientation and height still matter.

title: Practical Wideband Receiver Tips
body: Squelch mutes the receiver's noise output between transmissions on FM channels - set it just above the background noise floor so it opens cleanly when a real signal appears; squelch generally isn't used on AM/SSB signals, which fade in and out naturally. Tuning step matters: different services use different channel spacing (10 kHz for CB and AM broadcast, 12.5/15/20/25 kHz for various FM services, 5 kHz common on HF), so matching the receiver's tuning step to the service being searched makes scanning much faster. Expect nearby VHF/UHF transmitters to be far easier to copy clearly than distant or weak ones; HF signal strength, by contrast, can change noticeably minute to minute as propagation shifts.

title: What to Monitor During Severe Weather / an Emergency
body: Start with NOAA Weather Radio (162.400–162.550 MHz, NFM) for official forecasts and All Hazards alerts - it's the single most reliable receive-only source here. Locally, FRS/GMRS/MURS channels are commonly used for family/neighbor coordination during an outage. CB channel 9 (27.065 MHz) is the designated emergency channel and channel 19 (27.185 MHz) often carries road-condition chatter from truckers. If you're near water, marine VHF channel 16 (156.800 MHz) carries Coast Guard distress traffic and channel 22A (157.100 MHz) carries USCG safety/weather broadcasts. Amateur radio repeaters on 2m/70cm frequently carry organized emergency nets during major events, though monitoring them doesn't require a license - only transmitting does. This reference intentionally does not cover local public-safety/trunked radio systems - coverage is highly region-specific, many systems are digital/encrypted, and the legality of monitoring varies by state; check local resources for that specifically.

title: Decibels (dB / dBm) - Signal Strength Concepts
body: A decibel (dB) is a ratio, not an absolute amount - it compares two power levels on a logarithmic scale. +3 dB means roughly double the power; +10 dB means 10x the power; -3 dB means roughly half. dBm is an absolute unit built on the same scale: 0 dBm = 1 milliwatt, so +30 dBm = 1 watt, +40 dBm = 10 watts, and -100 dBm (a typical weak-signal receiver noise floor) is an extremely small fraction of a milliwatt. A receiver's signal-strength meter (often labeled S-units, S1-S9, then '+10/+20/+40 dB over S9' beyond that) is really just a coarse dB scale in disguise. The practical takeaway: doubling a radio's transmit power only gains about 3 dB - a genuinely modest, often barely-noticeable improvement - while a better antenna or feed line can easily gain far more than that for free.

title: Software-Defined Radio (SDR) Basics
body: A traditional radio does its filtering/demodulation in dedicated analog hardware built for one job. An SDR instead digitizes a chunk of raw spectrum as early as possible and does the rest - filtering, demodulation, decoding - in software, which is what makes a single device like a wideband receiver able to tune AM, FM, SSB, and digital modes across a huge frequency range without swapping hardware. The tradeoff is that an SDR's usable range at any instant is limited by its 'bandwidth' (how much spectrum it can digitize at once, distinct from the tuning range it can reach) and by its analog-to-digital converter's dynamic range (how well it handles a very strong nearby signal without swamping a weak one next to it - 'overload'). A 'waterfall' display is simply a visual history of that digitized spectrum over time, which is why SDR-based receivers are so good at showing activity across a whole band at a glance rather than one frequency at a time.

title: Simplex vs. Repeater Operation
body: Simplex means two stations talk directly to each other on one shared frequency - simple, but range is limited to whatever the two stations can reach directly (line-of-sight on VHF/UHF). A repeater instead listens on one frequency and instantly retransmits on a second frequency from a high, well-placed location (a hilltop or tall tower), so two low-power handheld radios that could never hear each other directly can both reach the repeater and therefore each other - dramatically extending practical range. This is why amateur 2m/70cm repeater listings always show two frequencies (input/output, often called the 'offset') rather than one, and why FRS/GMRS/MURS listings on this page are simplex-only (repeaters are a licensed-amateur/GMRS-specific concept, not available on unlicensed FRS/MURS). A repeater also usually requires a sub-audible tone (CTCSS) or digital code to activate ('open') it, which keeps it from responding to unrelated noise or distant repeaters sharing the same frequency pair.

title: Antenna Polarization
body: Polarization describes the orientation of a radio wave's electric field, and it's set by the physical orientation of the transmitting antenna - vertical (antenna standing straight up), horizontal (antenna lying flat), or circular (rotating, common for satellite/GPS work). Matching polarization between transmitter and receiver matters: a mismatch (vertical talking to horizontal) can weaken a signal by 20 dB or more, which is often the difference between a clear copy and hearing nothing at all. Convention, not physics, decides which is used where: VHF/UHF FM (repeaters, GMRS, FRS, most handhelds) is vertical by near-universal convention; broadcast FM/TV and many fixed point-to-point/amateur weak-signal links are horizontal; airband and most marine VHF are vertical. A handheld radio's antenna is vertical whenever the radio is held upright, which is exactly why it is - this alone is a large part of why matching a base or mobile antenna's orientation to what you're trying to hear noticeably improves reception.

title: Feed Lines & Common Connectors
body: The cable between a radio and its antenna (the 'feed line', almost always coax at these frequencies) loses some signal as heat over its length - loss increases with cable length, frequency, and cheaper/thinner cable, which is why a long run to an outdoor antenna benefits from thicker, lower-loss coax (e.g. RG-8/LMR-400 family) rather than thin RG-58, especially at VHF/UHF where loss per foot is much higher than at HF. Every connector in the path is also a potential loss/reflection point, so fewer adapters/barrel connectors in the chain is generally better. title: NATO Phonetic Alphabet
body: The standard spelling alphabet used internationally on radio and telephone to make letters unambiguous over a noisy channel (e.g. 'B' and 'D' sound alike, but 'Bravo' and 'Delta' don't). Officially the ICAO/NATO phonetic alphabet, but effectively universal across amateur, aviation, marine, and public-safety radio worldwide - one of the few things every radio service agrees on. For digits, the plain number names are normally used, though aviation/military contexts sometimes use 'niner' for 9 and 'fife' for 5 specifically to avoid confusion with similar-sounding words over a poor connection.

title: Morse Code Reference
body: International Morse Code - a series of short ('dit') and long ('dah', roughly 3x a dit's length) tones representing letters and digits. Still used today on amateur CW (Continuous Wave) sub-bands (see the CW entry under Modulation Types) because a Morse signal needs far less bandwidth and can be copied through noise/weak-signal conditions that would make voice unreadable. SOS (... --- ...) remains recognizable worldwide as a distress signal even to those with no other Morse knowledge, and is unusual among prosigns for being sent as one unbroken string rather than as three separate letters.
